nodes.label: Transport Layer
nodes.rationale: Provides logical communication between application processes on different hosts. The sender segments application messages and passes them to the network layer; the receiver reassembles segments and delivers them via sockets. Internet transport offers multiplexing, reliable data transfer, flow control, and congestion control, but not delay or bandwidth guarantees.

nodes.label: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach (9th edition)
nodes.rationale: Pearson 2025 textbook by Jim Kurose and Keith Ross. These slides are copyright 1996-2025 J.F. Kurose and K.W. Ross and are the Chapter 3 lecture deck.

nodes.label: Multiplexing
nodes.rationale: At the sender, data from multiple sockets is gathered and a transport header is added so the receiver can later demultiplex each segment to the correct socket.

nodes.label: Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: The receiver uses header fields to deliver a segment to the correct socket. Each IP datagram carries one transport segment; the host combines IP addresses with source and destination port numbers.

nodes.label: UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
nodes.rationale: Connectionless best-effort transport: segments may be lost or reordered, there is no handshake (so no extra RTT), no connection state, a small header, and no congestion control, so the sender can transmit as fast as desired and still function when the network is congested. Reliability and congestion control, if needed, are added in the application (as in HTTP/3).

nodes.label: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
nodes.rationale: Connection-oriented, point-to-point, full-duplex reliable in-order byte stream with no message boundaries. Handshake initializes sender and receiver state. Congestion control and flow control together set the pipeline window. MSS is the maximum segment size.

nodes.label: Reliable Data Transfer
nodes.rationale: Application sees a reliable channel even though the network channel may lose, corrupt, or reorder data. Sender and receiver do not know each other's state unless it is communicated. Complexity of the rdt protocol depends on the unreliable channel. Interfaces are rdt_send, udt_send, rdt_rcv, and deliver_data. FSMs specify the protocol; data is unidirectional while control flows both ways.

nodes.label: Flow Control
nodes.rationale: Keeps one sender from overflowing one receiver's socket buffer when the network delivers data faster than the application reads it. Distinct from congestion control, which limits many senders for the network's sake.

nodes.label: Congestion Control
nodes.rationale: Congestion is too many sources sending too much data too fast for the network, seen as long queueing delay and loss from router buffer overflow. Costs include extra retransmission work, unneeded duplicates that waste capacity, and upstream transmission wasted when a packet is dropped downstream. Throughput cannot exceed link capacity. It is a different problem from flow control.

nodes.label: Connectionless Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: UDP demultiplexes using only the destination port number. Datagrams with the same destination port but different source IP addresses or source ports are delivered to the same socket.

nodes.label: TCP Four-Tuple Demultiplexing
nodes.rationale: A TCP socket is identified by source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port. A server can hold many simultaneous sockets, and segments that share a destination IP and port (for example port 80) are demultiplexed to different sockets using the full 4-tuple.

nodes.label: Internet Checksum
nodes.rationale: Detects flipped bits. The sender treats the UDP segment, including header fields and IP addresses, as 16-bit integers and stores the one's complement sum, with end-around carry, in the checksum field. The receiver recomputes it. Equality does not prove the segment is error-free: some bit flips leave the checksum unchanged, so protection is weak.

nodes.label: UDP Segment Header
nodes.rationale: Four fields: source port, destination port, length in bytes of the UDP segment including the header, and checksum, followed by the application payload.

nodes.label: rdt1.0
nodes.rationale: Reliable transfer over a perfectly reliable channel: no bit errors and no packet loss. The sender puts data on the channel and the receiver reads it. Separate FSMs, no ACKs or retransmission.

nodes.label: rdt2.0
nodes.rationale: Channel may flip bits. Checksum detects errors. ACK means the packet was received OK; NAK means it had errors and the sender retransmits. Stop-and-wait: send one packet, then wait for the receiver response. A corrupted ACK or NAK is a fatal flaw because the sender cannot safely retransmit without risking duplicates.

nodes.label: rdt2.1
nodes.rationale: Handles garbled ACK/NAK by adding a sequence number. Alternating sequence numbers 0 and 1 suffice for stop-and-wait. The sender retransmits the current packet if ACK/NAK is corrupted; the receiver discards duplicates. Sender state must remember which sequence number is outstanding, so there are twice as many states. The receiver still cannot know whether its last ACK/NAK arrived.

nodes.label: rdt2.2
nodes.rationale: NAK-free equivalent of rdt2.1. Instead of a NAK, the receiver ACKs the last packet received OK and includes that sequence number. A duplicate ACK causes the sender to retransmit the current packet. TCP uses this approach.

nodes.label: rdt3.0
nodes.rationale: The channel can also lose data and ACKs. Checksums, sequence numbers, and ACKs are not enough. The sender starts a countdown timer and retransmits if no ACK arrives in a reasonable time. A delayed packet or ACK produces a duplicate, which sequence numbers already handle, so the ACK must name the packet. Stop-and-wait utilization is very low (example: 1 Gbps, 15 ms delay, 8000-bit packet yields Usender about 0.00027) because the protocol waits an RTT per packet.

nodes.label: Stop-and-Wait
nodes.rationale: The sender transmits one packet and waits for the receiver response before sending another. Correct but limits utilization of a high-bandwidth, long-delay channel to a small fraction of capacity.

nodes.label: Pipelining
nodes.rationale: The sender allows multiple in-flight, not-yet-acknowledged packets. Sequence-number range must grow and sender and/or receiver must buffer. Three-packet pipelining multiplies the stop-and-wait utilization example by about three.

nodes.label: Go-Back-N
nodes.rationale: Sender window of up to N consecutive unACKed packets with a k-bit sequence number. Cumulative ACK(n) acknowledges all packets through n and slides the window to n+1. One timer runs for the oldest in-flight packet; timeout(n) retransmits packet n and every higher packet still in the window. Receiver ACKs only the highest in-order packet (rcv_base) and may discard or buffer out-of-order packets; the extended FSM discards them and needs only expectedseqnum.

nodes.label: Selective Repeat
nodes.rationale: Receiver individually ACKs every correctly received packet and buffers out-of-order packets for in-order delivery. Sender keeps a timer per unACKed packet and retransmits only the packet that timed out, with at most N in flight. If the window is too large for the sequence space (example: sequence numbers 0-3 and window 3), a retransmission can fall inside the receiver window and be accepted as new data, because the receiver cannot see the sender's state.

nodes.label: TCP Segment Structure
nodes.rationale: Header fields include source and destination ports, sequence number (bytes in the bytestream, not segments), acknowledgement number (next expected byte, with the A bit), header length, receive window, Internet checksum, urgent pointer, options, and flags RST, SYN, FIN for connection management plus C and E for congestion notification.

nodes.label: TCP Sequence Numbers and Cumulative ACKs
nodes.rationale: Sequence number is the byte-stream number of the first data byte in the segment. An ACK carries the next byte expected from the other side and is cumulative. The telnet example shows Host A sending 'C' at Seq=42, ACK=79 and Host B echoing it at Seq=79, ACK=43. How the receiver treats out-of-order segments is not specified; it is up to the implementor.

nodes.label: TCP RTT Estimation and TimeoutInterval
nodes.rationale: Timeout must exceed RTT. Too short causes premature retransmission; too long reacts slowly to loss. SampleRTT measures transmission to ACK, ignoring retransmissions. EstimatedRTT is an EWMA with typical alpha 0.125. DevRTT is an EWMA of the absolute deviation with typical beta 0.25. TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4*DevRTT so the safety margin grows when RTT varies.

nodes.label: TCP Fast Retransmit
nodes.rationale: RFC 5681 ACK rules: delayed ACK up to 500 ms for a single in-order segment, an immediate cumulative ACK when a second in-order segment arrives, a duplicate ACK on a gap, and an immediate ACK when a segment fills a gap. Three duplicate ACKs mean later segments arrived, so the missing segment is likely lost and is retransmitted without waiting for timeout. A later cumulative ACK can also cover an earlier lost ACK.

nodes.label: TCP Receive Window (rwnd)
nodes.rationale: The receiver advertises free buffer space in the rwnd header field. RcvBuffer is set by socket options, typically defaulting to 4096 bytes, and many operating systems auto-adjust it. The sender limits unACKed in-flight data to the advertised rwnd so the receive buffer does not overflow.

nodes.label: Two-Way Handshake
nodes.rationale: req_conn(x) followed by acc_conn(x) does not always work. Variable delay, retransmission after loss, and reordering can leave a half-open connection with no client, or cause the server to accept duplicate data after it has forgotten x. Neither side can see the other.

nodes.label: TCP Three-Way Handshake
nodes.rationale: Before data, both sides agree to connect and agree on parameters such as initial sequence numbers. Client sends SYN (Seq=x) and enters SYN_SENT; server replies SYN-ACK (Seq=y, ACKnum=x+1) and enters SYN_RCVD; client sends ACK (ACKnum=y+1), which may carry data, and both reach ESTAB. Each ACK shows the other endpoint is live. Illustrated by the climbing exchange: On belay? / Belay on. / Climbing.

nodes.label: TCP Connection Teardown
nodes.rationale: Each side closes by sending a segment with FIN=1 and ACKing the peer's FIN. An ACK may be combined with its own FIN, and simultaneous FINs are allowed. The closing FSM uses FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK, CLOSING path states, and TIMED_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime before CLOSED.

nodes.label: AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease)
nodes.rationale: Senders increase the rate until loss, then decrease. Additive increase adds one MSS per RTT; multiplicative decrease cuts the rate in half on loss. The resulting sawtooth probes for bandwidth. AIMD is a distributed asynchronous algorithm shown to optimize congested flow rates network-wide and to have desirable stability properties.

nodes.label: TCP Tahoe
nodes.rationale: On loss detected by timeout, the sending rate is cut to 1 MSS rather than halved.

nodes.label: TCP Reno
nodes.rationale: On loss detected by a triple duplicate ACK, the sending rate is cut in half. Timeout still collapses the window to 1 MSS.

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Window (cwnd)
nodes.rationale: The sender limits transmission by LastByteSent - LastByteAcked < cwnd. cwnd is adjusted from observed congestion. Rough sending rate is cwnd/RTT bytes per second: send cwnd bytes, wait about one RTT for ACKs, then send more.

nodes.label: TCP Slow Start
nodes.rationale: At connection start cwnd is 1 MSS and doubles every RTT by incrementing cwnd on every ACK, so the initial rate is slow but the ramp is exponential. Growth switches to linear when cwnd reaches ssthresh, set on a loss event to half the cwnd just before the loss. The initial ssthresh shown in the FSM is 64 KB.

nodes.label: TCP Congestion Avoidance
nodes.rationale: Once cwnd exceeds ssthresh, each new ACK increases cwnd by MSS*(MSS/cwnd), which is about one MSS per RTT: linear probing rather than doubling.

nodes.label: TCP Fast Recovery
nodes.rationale: On a third duplicate ACK, ssthresh becomes cwnd/2, cwnd becomes ssthresh+3, and the missing segment is retransmitted. Further duplicate ACKs inflate cwnd by one MSS. A new ACK sets cwnd back to ssthresh and returns to congestion avoidance. A timeout from this state sets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start.

nodes.label: TCP CUBIC
nodes.rationale: Probes usable bandwidth using Wmax, the window at which congestion loss was last detected. After cutting the window in half, CUBIC increases W as a cubic function of the distance between the current time and K, the tunable time at which the window would again reach Wmax: larger steps far from K, smaller steps near K. It was the default in Linux and the most popular TCP on popular web servers until about 2024.

nodes.label: Bottleneck Link
nodes.rationale: Classic TCP and CUBIC raise the sending rate until some router output queue overflows. Once that link transmits at full rate R, a higher sending rate does not raise end-to-end throughput; it increases RTT through queueing delay. With N flows, each should ideally receive R/N. The design goal is to keep the end-to-end pipe just full, but not fuller.

nodes.label: Bandwidth-Delay Product
nodes.rationale: Ideal in-flight data for a connection is its share of bottleneck bandwidth times min_RTT. Below that product, more in-flight data does not increase RTT. Above it, arrival rate exceeds link rate, the buffer fills, and RTT grows. Loss-based TCP tends to operate at the full-buffer point.

nodes.label: BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT)
nodes.rationale: Seeks the just-full operating point rather than the loss-based full-buffer point by regulating ninflight. Acceleration raises rate until the throughput plateau; cruising sends at the rate ACKs show the network is delivering; deceleration reduces ninflight to ease the queue and look for a lower min_RTT. Over longer intervals it drains the pipe to remeasure min_RTT.

nodes.label: Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN)
nodes.rationale: Network-assisted congestion control, also exemplified by ATM and DECbit. Routers mark two bits in the IP ToS field under an operator-chosen policy. The mark is carried to the destination, which sets the ECE bit on the TCP ACK. Both IP ECN bits and TCP C,E bits are involved, so the sender learns congestion without waiting for loss. End-to-end control, used by TCP, instead infers congestion only from observed loss and delay, with no explicit network feedback.

nodes.label: TCP Fairness
nodes.rationale: If K TCP sessions share a bottleneck of bandwidth R, each should average R/K. Two sessions with additive increase of slope 1 and multiplicative decrease converge to equal shares under idealized assumptions: same RTT, fixed number of sessions, and congestion avoidance only. Fairness is not enforced: UDP multimedia can send at a constant rate and tolerate loss, and an application can open many parallel TCP connections (one connection gets R/10 beside nine others; eleven connections get about R/2). There is no Internet police for congestion control.

nodes.label: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections)
nodes.rationale: Application-layer protocol on UDP that takes on connection establishment, error control, and congestion control to speed HTTP. Many application streams share one QUIC connection, each with its own reliable transfer, while congestion control is common, so a loss does not head-of-line block other streams the way TCP reliable delivery does under HTTP/1.1. Reliability, congestion control, authentication, encryption, and state can be established in one RTT or even zero. Deployed on many Google servers and apps, including Chrome and the mobile YouTube app. The QUIC specification notes that its loss detection and congestion control parallel well-known TCP algorithms.

nodes.label: HTTP/3
nodes.rationale: Runs over UDP via QUIC. When reliable transfer is needed over UDP, reliability and congestion control are added at the application layer rather than by TCP. The stack contrast is HTTP/2 over TCP plus TLS versus a slimmed HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over UDP and QUIC.

nodes.label: SNMP
nodes.rationale: Used as the running example of UDP sender and receiver actions: the SNMP message is placed in a UDP segment, passed to IP, checksum-checked, and demultiplexed to the socket.

nodes.label: TCP RFCs 793, 1122, 2018, 5681, and 7323
nodes.rationale: The overview of TCP points to these RFCs for the protocol, host requirements, selective acknowledgement, congestion control, and window scale.

nodes.label: RFC 5681
nodes.rationale: Cited specifically for TCP receiver ACK generation, including delayed ACKs and duplicate ACKs.

nodes.label: Kelly congestion-control optimality result
nodes.rationale: Cited for the result that AIMD optimizes congested flow rates network-wide and has desirable stability properties. The slides name Kelly without a year or title.

nodes.label: Mathis 1997 TCP throughput model
nodes.rationale: Average TCP throughput is about 3/4 W per RTT when loss occurs at window W, ignoring slow start. In terms of segment loss probability L, throughput is about 1.22 * MSS / (RTT * sqrt(L)). A 10 Gbps target with 1500-byte segments and 100 ms RTT needs on the order of 83,333 in-flight segments and a loss rate of about 2e-10, which motivates TCP versions for long, high-speed pipes.
